entities.name: Tettius Julianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Tettius Julianus, a distinguished Roman general and politician, played a pivotal role in the early stages of Rome's conflicts with the Dacians during the Flavian dynasty. His career, spanning the reigns of Vespasian, Titus, and most notably Domitian, saw him rise through the imperial ranks, culminating in his suffect consulship in 83 CE and a critical command on the Danubian frontier. Julianus's actions provided a significant, albeit temporary, check to the burgeoning power of the Dacian king Decebalus, shaping the strategic landscape that Trajan would later inherit.

His military acumen was most prominently displayed during the First Dacian War (86–88 CE). Following the devastating defeat of Cornelius Fuscus at Tapae in 86 CE, Tettius Julianus was appointed commander of the Roman forces in Moesia Superior. In 88 CE, he led a decisive campaign against Decebalus, marching his legions through the formidable Iron Gates pass and achieving a significant victory over the Dacians once again at Tapae. This triumph avenged the earlier Roman losses and demonstrated the continued strength of the Roman military machine, despite the political and strategic complexities introduced by Emperor Domitian's policies.

Although Julianus's victory at Tapae was a military success, it did not lead to the complete subjugation of Dacia under Domitian, who instead negotiated a controversial peace treaty. Nevertheless, his campaign underscored the strategic importance of the Danubian frontier and provided invaluable intelligence and experience that would inform Trajan's more ambitious and ultimately successful Dacian Wars a decade later. Julianus's achievements solidified Roman control over vital border regions and temporarily stabilized a volatile frontier, preventing further Dacian incursions into Roman territory.
